Hello from Uruguay! 🇺🇾🚀

We are Las Hackers, a team of students from Santa Elena School in Uruguay, excited to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge! 🌎✨
summary: From the Moon to Mars is a hands-on educational model with narration audio that tells the story of human and robotic space exploration. Our team built a physical diorama that shows a lunar surface and a Martian surface side by side, with 3D-printed parts, LED lights and Lego-style robots that represent rovers. The narration guides the audience through the Apollo 11 mission, the objects humanity has left on other worlds, the history of Mars rovers from Sojourner to Perseverance, and the next step: learning to live and work on the Moon to prepare for humans on Mars. Our project makes space exploration easy to understand for children and families by combining something you can see and touch with a story you can hear. We believe that inspiring young people today is how we prepare the explorers who will one day travel to Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works. Our project is a physical model divided into two landscapes: the gray, cratered surface of the Moon and the red, rocky surface of Mars, set against a starry background. Electric LED lights represent stars and planets, and Lego-style blocks are used to build small space robots and astronauts. A narration audio explains each part of the model while people look at it, and we also recorded a video of the model to share it online.

The story we tell. The narration covers the Apollo 11 mission (the Saturn V launch on July 16, 1969, the Columbia command module and the Eagle lunar module, and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin’s walk on the Moon on July 20, 1969); what humans have left behind on the Moon and Mars; the robots that explore Mars because no human has gone there yet (Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance, which in October 2026 set the record for the longest distance driven on another world); and why the Moon is the training ground for future missions to Mars.

Benefits and intended impact. The model helps children and visitors understand the connection between the past, present and future of space exploration. Combining a physical model with audio makes the experience accessible to people who learn better by seeing, listening or touching.

Tools and materials. 3D-printed parts, a lightweight frame, handmade lunar and Martian surfaces, electric LED lights, Lego-style blocks, a narration audio recording, and Canva for the presentation and video.

Creativity. Instead of only showing pictures, we built a small world where the Moon and Mars meet, so the audience can “travel” from one to the other while listening to the story.

Factors we considered. Making the surfaces look realistic, using durable and lightweight materials, choosing accurate historical facts, and keeping the story simple enough for young audiences.
